analysis.one_liner: Bars forced arbitration and class-action waivers for workplace age discrimination claims.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee with no cosponsors and never received a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Most employment contracts require workers to settle disputes in private arbitration rather than court, and bar them from joining together in class actions. This bill would let a worker age 40 or older who claims age discrimination — including harassment, retaliation, or unequal pay — take the case to a judge instead, regardless of what their contract says. It applied only to new claims and did not touch arbitration for any other kind of dispute.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers age 40 and older with age discrimination claims. They could sue in court, have a judge decide whether the contract applies, and join class actions instead of arguing alone before an arbitrator.

how_it_helps.text: Renders predispute arbitration agreements and predispute joint-action waivers unenforceable, at the worker's election, for any case involving age discrimination under federal, state, tribal, or local law [S2][S3].
Requires a court, not an arbitrator, to decide whether the ban applies, even if the contract purports to delegate that question to an arbitrator [S3].
Covers disparate treatment, disparate impact, harassment, and retaliation, and applies to class or collective action representatives [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers lose a major shield: they could no longer use standard employment contracts to keep age discrimination cases out of court or prevent employees from joining together. Arbitration providers and the firms that defend employers in arbitration would lose that stream of cases.

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is that arbitration is faster and cheaper for workers than litigation, and the bill lets the worker choose — but only after a dispute arises, meaning employers lose certainty in drafting employment contracts, a real cost they would argue is borne by consumers and investors [S3].

The bill leaves arbitration in place for every other type of employment dispute, so its benefit is limited to a single category of claims rather than reforming forced arbitration across the board [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to older workers is real and direct: court access and the ability to join together, which the 2022 law already did for sexual harassment claims, extended here to age claims. The cost falls on employers in the form of more litigation exposure, which is exactly the point of the bill. The main design weakness is its narrow scope, not any burden on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, the committee never acted on it, and it expired at the end of the 118th Congress.

narrative.text: Representative Nancy Mace introduced the bill on June 14, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary [S5].
No further action was ever taken: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no House floor vote, and it had no cosponsors [S4][S5].

The bill's title mirrors the protection Congress enacted for sexual harassment claims in the 2022 Ending Forced Arbitration of Sexual Assault and Sexual Harassment Act, extended here to age discrimination claims under 40-plus federal age bias law [S2].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers keep the ability to route age discrimination claims into arbitration and block class actions, and arbitration providers keep the business. Workers over 40 gained nothing from the bill's death — they remain bound by the arbitration clauses in their contracts.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers with arbitration clauses in contracts

against.name: House Judiciary Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote on the bill after it was referred.

against.name: 429 House members
against.what_they_did: None joined as cosponsors during the two-year life of the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The sole sponsor was a Republican and no other member of either party signed on, so the bill's partisan shape is a lone sponsor rather than a party split.

industries.industry: Employers (especially large workplaces with mandatory arbitration clauses)
industries.note: Mandatory arbitration agreements and class-action waivers let employers resolve age bias claims privately and individually, without juries or public records. The bill would have stripped that shield for age discrimination claims, so its defeat keeps their current position intact.

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and defense-side employment law practices
industries.note: The bill would have redirected age discrimination disputes from private arbitration toward the courts, removing a significant volume of employer-side arbitration work. The bill's defeat preserves that business.
